text: Let $S_{k}=\sum\limits _{r=1}^{k}\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{6^{r}}{2^{2r+1}+3^{2r+1}}\right )$. Then $\lim _{k\to \infty }S_{k}$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 16th March Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$S_{k} =$ $\sum\limits _{r=1}^{k}\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{6^{r}(3-2)}{\left (1+\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{2r+1}\right )2^{2r+1}}\right )$

= $\sum\limits _{r=1}^{k}\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{2^{r}.3^{r+1}-3^{r}2^{r+1}}{\left (1+\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{2r+1}\right )2^{2r+1}}\right )$

= $\sum\limits _{r=1}^{k}\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{r+1}-\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{r}}{1+\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{r+1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{r}}\right )$

= $\sum\limits _{r=1}^{k}\left [\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{r+1}-\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{r}\right ]$

= $\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{2}-\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{1}$

+ $\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{3}-\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{2}$

+ $\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{4}-\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{3}$

.

.

.

+ $\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{k+1}-\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{k}$

= $\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{k+1}-\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{1}$

$\therefore$ $\lim _{k\to \infty }S_{k}$

= $\lim _{k\to \infty }\left [\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{k+1}-\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )^{1}\right ]$

= $\tan ^{-1}(\infty )-\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )$

= $\frac{π}{2}-\tan ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )$

= $\cot ^{-1}\left (\frac{3}{2}\right )$

text: Let $A=\left [\begin{array}{ll} i & -i \\ -i & i \end{array}\right ],i=\sqrt{-1}$. Then, the system of linear equations $A^{8}\left [\begin{array}{l} x \\ y \end{array}\right ]=\left [\begin{array}{l} 8 \\ 64 \end{array}\right ]$ has :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 16th March Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$A=\left [\begin{array}{ll} i & -i \\ -i & i \end{array}\right ]$

$A^{2}=\left [\begin{array}{ll} i & -i \\ -i & i \end{array}\right ]\left [\begin{array}{ll} i & -i \\ -i & i \end{array}\right ]=\left [\begin{array}{ll} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{array}\right ]=2\left [\begin{array}{ll} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{array}\right ]$

$A^{4}=4\left [\begin{array}{ll} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{array}\right ]\left [\begin{array}{ll} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{array}\right ]=4\left [\begin{array}{ll} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{array}\right ]=8\left [\begin{array}{ll} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{array}\right ]$

$A^{8}=64\left [\begin{array}{ll} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{array}\right ]\left [\begin{array}{ll} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{array}\right ]=64\left [\begin{array}{ll} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{array}\right ]=128\left [\begin{array}{ll} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{array}\right ]$

$128\left [\begin{array}{ll} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{array}\right ]\left [\begin{array}{l} x \\ y \end{array}\right ]=\left [\begin{array}{l} 8 \\ 64 \end{array}\right ]$

$128\left [\begin{array}{l} x-y \\ -x+y \end{array}\right ]=\left [\begin{array}{l} 8 \\ 64 \end{array}\right ]$

$\Rightarrow 128(x-y)=8$

$\Rightarrow x-y=\frac{1}{16}$ .... (1)

and $128(-x+y)=64\Rightarrow x-y=\frac{-1}{2}$ .... (2)

$\Rightarrow$ No solution (from eq. (1) & (2))

text: Consider an arithmetic series and a geometric series having four initial terms from the set {11, 8, 21, 16, 26, 32, 4}. If the last terms of these series are the maximum possible four digit numbers, then the number of common terms in these two series is equal to $___________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 16th March Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The four terms in A.P. are $11,16,21,26$ (common difference $5$) and the four terms in G.P. are $4,8,16,32$ (common ratio $2$).

The A.P. terms are $11+5k$; the largest four-digit one is $11+5\times 1997=9996$. So the A.P. is $11,16,21,\ldots ,9996$: every number from $11$ to $9996$ that leaves remainder $1$ on division by $5$.

The G.P. terms are $2^{m}$; the largest four-digit one is $2^{13}=8192$. So the G.P. is $2^{m}$ for $m=2,3,\ldots ,13$.

The remainders of $2^{m}$ on division by $5$ repeat as $2,4,3,1$ for $m=1,2,3,4$, so $2^{m}$ leaves remainder $1$ only when $m$ is a multiple of $4$.

For $2\leq m\leq 13$ this gives $m=4,8,12$, i.e. the common terms $16,256,4096$, all lying between $11$ and $9996$.

Hence, the answer is 3.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2021 (Online) 16th March Morning Shift

For this limit to exist

text: Let z and $ω$ be two complex numbers such that $ω=zz–-2z+2,\left |\frac{z+i}{z-3i}\right |=1$ and Re($ω$) has minimum value. Then, the minimum value of n $\in$ N for which $ω^{n}$ is real, is equal to $______________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 16th March Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let z = x + iy

| z + i | = | z $-$ 3i |

$\Rightarrow$ y = 1

Now 

$ω$ $= x^{2} + y^{2}$ $-$ 2x $-$ 2iy + 2

$ω$ $= x^{2} + 1$ $-$ 2x $-$ 2i + 2

Re($ω) = x^{2}$ $-$ 2x + 3

Re($ω$) = (x $-$ $1)^{2} + 2$

Re($ω)_{\min }$ at x = 1 $\Rightarrow$ z = 1 + i

Now, 

$ω$ = 1 + 1 $-$ 2 $-$ 2i + 2

$ω$ = 2(1 $-$ i) = 2$\sqrt{2}e^{i\left (\frac{-π}{4}\right )}$

$ω^{n}$ = 2$\sqrt{2}e^{i\left (\frac{-nπ}{4}\right )}$

If $ω^{n}$ is real $\Rightarrow$ n = 4

text: The total number of 3 $\times$ 3 matrices A having entries from the set {0, 1, 2, 3} such that the sum of all the diagonal entries of $AA^{T}$ is 9, is equal to $_____________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2021 (Online) 16th March Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$AA^{T}=\left [\begin{array}{lll} x & y & z \\ a & b & c \\ d & e & f \end{array}\right ]\left [\begin{array}{lll} x & a & d \\ y & b & e \\ z & c & f \end{array}\right ]$

$=\left [\begin{array}{lll} x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2} & ax+by+cz & dx+ey+fz \\ ax+by+cz & a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2} & ad+be+cf \\ dx+ey+fz & ad+be+cf & d^{2}+e^{2}+f^{2} \end{array}\right ]$

$Tr(AA^{T})=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}+a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}+e^{2}+f^{2}=9$

Case-I : Nine ones = 1 case

Case-II : 8 zeroes and one entry is 3 =  $\frac{9!}{8!}=9$ cases

Case-III : Two 2’s, one 1’s and 6 zeroes = $\frac{9!}{2!6!}=63\times 4=252$

Case IV : one 2, five 1, rest 0 $\frac{9!}{5!3!}=63\times 8=504$

$\therefore$ Total cases = 9 + 252 + 504 + 1 = 766
